llm.summary: FounderClaw broadly matches its stated purpose (a multi-agent engineering toolkit that runs a local browser daemon and installs several helper skills), but there are several red flags you should verify before installing—most notably a curl|bash remote installer, prompt-injection patterns in the SKILL.md, and access to sensitive browser cookies/keychain and local files.

dimensions.detail: The repo contents (browser daemon, Chrome extension, many skill SKILL.md files) are consistent with the claimed multi-agent engineering toolkit. The large set of files (browse daemon, extension code, install/uninstall scripts) matches the described capabilities (headless/headed browser, cookie import, QA workflows). Minor incoherence: the registry metadata marks this as 'instruction-only' with no install spec, yet the bundle contains an install.sh and many source files — not necessarily malicious but worth noting.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md explicitly tells users to run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ashish797/FounderClaw/main/install.sh | bash — i.e., download and execute a remote script. The instructions also describe actions that touch sensitive local state (copying Chromium cookie DBs, prompting macOS Keychain access, writing logs and eval artifacts under ~/.founderclaw-dev or founderclaw/data). Those actions are within the tool's functional scope (browser-based QA), but executing remote install scripts and automatic log collection raise privacy/risk concerns. The SKILL.md also contains a detected 'system-prompt-override' pattern (prompt-injection signal) which could indicate embedded text that attempts to influence agent/system prompts — this is unexpected and should be reviewed.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no formal install spec in the registry metadata, but SKILL.md recommends executing a raw GitHub-hosted install.sh via a curl|bash pipeline. While raw.githubusercontent.com is a common host, piping external scripts directly into a shell is high-risk because it executes remote code with user privileges. The repository also includes install.sh and many source files and a Chrome extension, so prefer reviewing the included install.sh and other scripts locally before running them. No archive downloads from obscure hosts were detected, but automatic execution is the main risk.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required environment variables or credentials, which matches the registry metadata. The SKILL.md documents optional use of ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for certain tests and describes accessing local browser cookie DBs and OS keychain (macOS, GNOME Keyring) with explicit user approval. Requesting keychain access and reading cookie DBs is sensitive but proportionate to a browser-testing tool — however you should expect explicit prompts and verify that cookies/keys are only accessed with your consent, and review the code that performs key access and cookie decryption before trusting it.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is not configured as always:true (no forced global persistence) and is user-invocable. Installing founderclaw will create files and directories under user home (e.g., ~/.founderclaw/, ~/.agents/skills/, ~/.founderclaw-dev/) and may modify OpenClaw config and create symlinks as part of dev-mode setup; that is expected for this kind of tool but you should review the install steps and confirm promotions to modify configs. There is no explicit sign it tries to change other skills' credentials, but the 'proactive' suggestion feature will cause it to suggest skills when installed.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
Before installing FounderClaw, do these checks:

1) Do NOT run curl ... | bash blindly. Instead fetch the install script (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ashish797/FounderClaw/main/install.sh) into a local file, inspect it, and run it only after you understand what it will change (files, symlinks, services, config edits). Prefer cloning the repo and running the local install.sh so you can audit it.

2) Review install.sh, uninstall.sh, and any scripts referenced by them for commands that modify global configs, restart services, or spawn background daemons. If you see network calls, remote exec, or privilege escalations, be cautious.

3) Inspect the code that reads/decrypts browser cookies and the keychain-access code to confirm it prompts you and does not exfiltrate secrets. The project documents copying cookie DBs and using the OS keychain — verify cookies and keys are not logged or sent to external endpoints.

4) Audit the Chrome extension code (extension/*) and any network endpoints (e.g., landing page URLs) to ensure they don't POST sensitive data to remote servers. The repo references GitHub and a landing URL; confirm these are legitimate and match the author.

5) Examine the SKILL.md sections flagged for prompt-injection/system-prompt override. Make sure no part of the skill attempts to override agent/system prompts or embed deceptive instructions that would alter the platform-level behavior.

6) If you need to try it, run the install in a contained environment (VM or throwaway account) first, or at minimum backup relevant config files (~/.openclaw, ~/.agents, any config the installer will edit). Keep the uninstall.sh handy and check what it removes.

If you are not comfortable auditing the scripts or code, avoid installing or only run in an isolated environment. If you do proceed, limit what model/keys you expose (do not put production credentials into .env for evaluation) and be prepared to revoke access if anything looks off.
llm.findings: [system-prompt-override] unexpected: The SKILL.md contains patterns flagged as 'system-prompt-override' by the static scanner. Skills that attempt to manipulate system prompts or inject instructions into agent/system-level prompts are unexpected for a repo whose primary functionality is browser automation and multi-agent workflows. Inspect these sections to ensure they are not trying to override agent/system prompts or perform prompt-injection.
